# Diagnosing Low Beam Failure While High Beams Function on a 2006 Chevy HHR

When both high beams illuminate correctly but the low beams fail completely, you are looking at a specific circuit isolation issue rather than a total bulb failure or generator fault. In the context of a 2006 Chevy HHR, this symptom pattern strongly suggests that the fuse for the low beam circuit has blown, or there is an open switch within the headlight assembly itself. Since high beams share power sources but operate on separate circuits controlled by different relays and fuses, their functionality confirms your battery, alternator, main harness ground, and the left/right side of the vehicle's lighting module are likely intact.

The most common point of failure in this configuration is the multi-fuse relay center located under the dashboard or in the engine bay compartment, depending on whether it is an early or late model production run of the HHR. You should immediately locate the fuse box diagram specific to your VIN year and trim level. Look for fuses labeled "Low Beam," "Headlight," or "Horn" (depending on how GM routed power in that chassis). If you have a multimeter, set it to continuity mode and test the suspected fuse. A blown low beam fuse will show infinite resistance, whereas the high beam fuse should read near zero ohms. Replacing a blown fuse is the lowest-friction solution, but if the new fuse blows immediately upon reinstallation, do not keep cycling power; this indicates a short circuit downstream that requires further investigation to prevent fire hazards.

If the fuses are intact, the issue likely lies within the headlight assembly's internal switch or wiring harness. The 2006 HHR uses projector-style headlights which contain complex relay logic inside the housing itself. When you flip the dial from "Off" to "Low," a specific pin in the connector activates the low-beam filaments while disabling the high-beam relay. If both low beams are dead but the unit works for highs, the internal switch that toggles between these states may have corroded or failed mechanically. In many cases, the black plastic housing around the bulb socket also contains a thermal fuse or a moisture seal that can degrade over time due to road salt and humidity, causing an open circuit specifically in the low-beam terminals.

To isolate this without fully disassembling the headlight, you can perform a jumper test. Carefully disconnect the electrical connector at the back of the headlight assembly while the vehicle is off. Using insulated probes or a temporary extension wire, apply 12V power directly to the low beam terminal pins identified in your wiring diagram. If the bulbs light up with this direct connection, the headlight bulb and socket are good, confirming the fault resides in the vehicle's side of the harness or the internal switch. This method effectively rules out a failed bulb assembly without needing to replace expensive projector units yet.

Another potential culprit is the headlight relay located in the under-hood fuse panel. While high beams often have their own dedicated relay, some configurations share a common power feed that gets switched differently by the dimmer stalk. Check for any relays labeled "Headlight" or "PRLY" and swap them with an identical known-good relay from another slot to see if functionality transfers. If the problem persists across multiple fuse checks, jumper tests, and relay swaps, the internal wiring harness of the headlight assembly itself is likely compromised due to age-related cracking in the plastic insulation inside the housing.

At this stage, replacing the entire headlight assembly or repairing the internal harness is often more cost-effective than sourcing individual components for a 2006 model year vehicle. However, before purchasing new parts, ensure you have verified that the ground strap from the headlight to the chassis frame isn't corroded. A poor ground can kill low beams while allowing highs to function if their return path differs slightly in resistance. If all electrical diagnostics point to a solid connection but no power reaches the bulb terminals, the internal switch within the projector lens assembly has failed, necessitating a unit replacement or professional repair by an auto-electrician familiar with GM projector logic.
